blocks.cap: Lead image for the article (Image: Deadline)

blocks.x: Seedance 2.5, ByteDance's video generation model, has started refusing prompts that directly reproduce Hollywood IP and the faces of stars.
The earlier Seedance 2.0 drew heavy criticism after deepfake videos made of Tom Cruise and Brad Pitt spread online. This move comes in the wake of that episode.

It's rare to see IP and likeness guardrails bolted onto a mainstream video model that creators actually use after the fact. For anyone working with Seedance, what prompts get through is about to change.

blocks.cap: Still from Daniel Roher and Charlie Tyrell's THE AI DOC: OR HOW I BECAME AN APOCALOPTIMIST (Photo: Focus Features)

blocks.x: When watching news or documentaries, audiences need to be able to trust the footage on screen. Yet widely used video editing software increasingly includes AI features that even directors themselves aren't aware of, and they're even less aware of how to turn them off.

An upcoming seminar addresses this concern. It will teach journalists and documentary filmmakers when to remove AI and exactly how to do it. IndieWire has learned exclusively that Field of Vision and the Freedom of the Press Foundation are launching the sixth installment of their Digital Security Clinic, a free online course series covering the digital footprint of documentary crews and journalists. It has supported more than 500 production teams over five-plus years, and this installment has already surpassed last year's in pre-registration interest.

The headline of this installment is a new session set for September 10 called “When and How to Opt Out of AI.” Field of Vision co-founder Charlotte Cook said it's a topic users have long requested. She's wary of tools that pull AI in through less visible means, like autocorrect or search engine integration. The point, she said, is for creators to know their process precisely and be able to prove what they authored — for the sake of audiences who need to trust the media, too.

Cook put it this way: “Filmmakers need to be able to safeguard the images and footage they work with, and to know that no influence they're unaware of has crept in, so they can stand behind the result.”

In the session, Freedom of the Press trainers walk participants through it step by step. That includes how to turn off specific AI features in editing tools and apps, where to upload footage while protecting it from AI crawling, and how to tell whether something has been altered or edited. “It's the risk assessment you need when evaluating AI tools and seeing what connects to what and how,” Cook summed up. It also covers transcription services and protecting intellectual property, including confirming that it's truly yours. She said some tools are changing their user policies, making where ownership actually lies the challenge of the moment.

This is one of five sessions held over the course of a month. The others cover digital security, how to communicate safely across borders or in sensitive regions, secure storage and encryption of footage, and reducing your digital footprint, including deleting private material from personal social accounts.

The schedule is as follows: August 13, Getting Started with Digital Security; August 20, Communicating Safely; August 27, Protecting Footage; September 3, Reducing Your Digital Footprint; September 10, AI Opt-Out. All sessions run Thursdays from 1:30 to 3 p.m.
Field of Vision keeps related materials and guides at https://www.digitalsecurity.film/. Sign-ups for group training are being taken at bit.ly/digitalsecurity2026.

blocks.cap: 〈Rainbow Hollow〉 (Image: Nura Studios)

blocks.x: 〈Rainbow Hollow〉 looks like stop-motion. It isn't. This adult dark comedy series, directed by Noah Wagner, made every shot with AI. It's the first original from Nura Studios, which opened its doors in April.

It started at a funeral. Watching a friend's coffin lowered into the ground, Wagner thought there was no good way to lay out a body. He wrote down the scene that came to him at the time in his production journal: a camera follows the coffin down and lingers beside the corpse, then there's a knock and an undead creature pokes its head in.

It was claymation from the start. He wrote that it wasn't a decision reached afterward — the scene that came to him was claymation itself. But he had neither the resources nor the industry backing to pull off real stop-motion at this scale. He describes the series' visual style as a debt owed to that craft, not a replacement for it. “There's nothing that replaces that soul and that human connection,” he said.

Milo is a firefighter who died too soon trying to save a cat stuck in a tree. Buried in the ground, he discovers Rainbow Hollow, a town where the dead keep on living, on one condition: the body has to stay intact. When Milo learns his wife wants to be cremated, he sets out to kill her, both for her sake and so the two of them can stay together forever.

Robert Koscheleon voices Milo, and Art Brown voices Lazarus. Michael Koehler wrote the script and built the series together with Wagner. Wagner also handled animation and editing, and the two split the original idea into three episodes. Isabel Riva is executive producer, and Graziela LaRocca is technical producer. 〈Rainbow Hollow〉 is a co-production between Nura and A Work of Ark.

blocks.cap: Lazarus (Image: Nura Studios)

blocks.x: The production foundation is Showcraft, a web platform for making animated episodes that Nura unveiled in April and has spent the following months testing in a private beta. It brings story, preproduction, layout, animation, editing, and post finishing together in one environment built on fine-tuned AI models. Wagner explains that it replaces AI filmmaking that used to run across scattered folders and canvases with a single interface that carries through from shot to shot. Feedback from creators on-site flows into the platform in real time.

Writing took a month. The roughly seven weeks that followed had generation and editing running side by side rather than in sequence. Most of it was made with Seedance 2.0, which he says held onto the rough claymation texture and pulled lip-sync straight from actor recordings. He attached shots to the sequence first, then decided what the next shot should be. “The actual film was 100% discovered and made in the edit,” he wrote.

The beta participant list included Bento Box Entertainment co-founder Joel Kuwahara, former Disney visual development artist John Mahoney, and former Pixar cinematographer Jerica Cleland. Ervin Han, who won the feature Crystal at 2026 Annecy with Raúl García for 〈The Violinist〉, also took part.

Showcraft opens to the public in early September. Other Nura series will follow in August and September. Wagner serves as head producer of AI and innovation at Ecobend Creative, and his work has aired on HBO, Netflix, NBC, and BBC.

blocks.x: ActionVFX has launched an online course called “VFX for Filmmakers.” It's designed for video professionals who aren't VFX specialists — directors, editors, cinematographers, and solo creators — to produce substantial visual effects on their own for commercials, music videos, and indie films.

As client expectations rise and production budgets shrink, video professionals in the field increasingly find themselves handling visual effects without a dedicated VFX studio. The course pairs traditional directing sense with a complete compositing pipeline, teaching how to produce studio-grade shots with software people already have, like Adobe After Effects and Photoshop.

The curriculum comes with a professional asset bundle worth $2,300. Students receive 13 live-action practice plates to follow along with the lessons, more than 50 ActionVFX Pro elements, and a practical VFX reference guide.

ActionVFX CEO Rodolphe Pierre-Louis said: “Most filmmakers hit a wall the moment a shot needs visual effects. They either scale back their creative vision or burn the budget on outsourcing — it's one or the other. This course changes that equation. It gives directors, cinematographers, and editors a repeatable pipeline so they can shoot smarter on set, use practical AI tools, and produce client-ready shots without a VFX department.”

The course is led by ActionVFX production veterans Zachery Vanhoy and Sam Crowe. It's structured to take students from zero experience to delivering a finished, professional shot, stripping away theoretical padding to focus on situations that actually matter in practice.

The production asset bundle, worth more than $2,300, includes 13 live-action practice plates, around 50 ActionVFX stock elements, project files, and an on-set reference cheat sheet. The module linking set and post covers previsualization, green screen lighting, camera setup, tracking markers, and on-set data collection, eliminating post-production headaches before the software is even opened.

The project-based learning centers on a hero green screen composite set against a matte painting environment, with separate mini-projects for sky replacement (point tracking) and screen replacement (planar tracking). The “Modern AI Integration” module teaches depth map generation, AI-assisted rotoscoping, content-aware fill, and LLM-assisted technical troubleshooting as practical tools. Students progress at their own pace.
“VFX for Filmmakers” is currently open for $299.

blocks.cap: Artlist heavily advertised Seedance 2.5 as “1-year unlimited,” then cut off access within a week (screenshot: Reddit).

blocks.x: All weekend, Artlist told filmmakers that buying an annual AI Creator subscription would get them unlimited use of ByteDance's Seedance 2.5 for twelve months. Days later, the model was pulled from the unlimited list on every plan, and people who had paid around $500 were given credits worth a small fraction of that. Artlist says demand was the problem. Looking at the model's own per-unit cost, it was a promise the company couldn't have kept from the start.

Credit where it's due: the company stopped hiding behind euphemism. In a statement sent to affected customers, it said it made a big promise it “could not deliver on” and acknowledged the mistake. That's the most honest sentence to come out of Artlist this week — and also an admission that the offer was sold without anyone checking whether it was deliverable.

Seedance 2.5 isn't a cheap model to serve. On the public reseller market, generating one second of 720p video runs around $0.47, putting the cost of a single 30-second clip at roughly $14. Artlist's promotional terms capped daily use at about 2,550 seconds — 85 clips of 30 seconds each. Multiply that out and one heavy-use subscriber burns through about $1,190 worth of inference a day. On a $500-a-year subscription.

Artlist's wholesale pricing isn't public, so this figure only shows direction, and it doesn't need to be precise. Plug in whatever discount rate you like, and a single heavy user recoups a full year's subscription fee in a single day, leaving the company losing money for the remaining 364 days. This wasn't a miscalculated forecast — it was an offer that only worked if customers didn't use what they bought. Customers used it, and it collapsed within a week.
The number 2,550 seconds tells its own story: the unlimited plan had a daily cap built in from the moment it was sold.

blocks.cap: The message Artlist sent subscribers announcing the end of Seedance 2.5 access (screenshot provided by a user).

blocks.x: If the whole industry had hit the same wall, blaming capacity might have held up — but it didn't. Higgsfield capped unlimited at a maximum of 33 days; Runway gives new Max subscribers 7 days; Renoise offers a week; Topview offers 60 days; Krea works in 7-, 15-, or 30-day increments; OpenArt ties unlimited to 5-second, 480p generations. That's as far as the economics hold up. Only Artlist sold 365 days, and marketed that gap not as a warning sign but as proof of value.

The terms define unlimited as “not deducting credits for that generation during the access period,” then strip nearly all meaning out of the word. Language guaranteeing nothing about speed, capacity, uninterrupted access, number of generations, or “continued provision of AI services, models, or features” stayed live on the site even while the promotion was running. The legal defense line was already drawn before the marketing ever went out.

The remedy was designed to protect cash. Affected subscribers' monthly credits rose from 80,000 to 180,000. AI Creator costs $41.67 a month billed annually, or $69.99 billed monthly, and users say they paid $499.99 for the promotional annual plan. By customers' own math, a 30-second generation costs about 15,000 credits, which means the upgraded allowance works out to a little over twelve clips a month. What had been 85 a day became twelve a month.

The fairest remedy, a refund, is opt-in only, and limited to buyers who purchased between August 7 and 10. Customers have to seek it out, request it, and wait. Some were processed quickly as policy promised; many others, blocked by refusals or silence, got their money back through PayPal or card-issuer chargebacks instead.

Each suite comes with more than 25 pre-configured workflows, a cloud-native SaaS architecture, managed deployment options, open APIs, and built-in AI features. blocks.cap: Nvidia AI video detector (image: NVIDIA)

blocks.x: Nvidia has released a tool for identifying AI-generated content.
The Synthetic Video Detector NIM microservice, built into the NVIDIA For Media platform, breaks video down frame by frame and outputs a classification score for whether synthetic content is mixed in.

The judgment holds up even after the compression, resizing, cropping, and re-encoding common in newsroom and social video work. In Nvidia's own testing, accuracy reached up to 92% on uncompressed video, 87% at 15% compression, and 82% at 50% compression.
Processing speed, for 1080p, is 22 milliseconds on NVIDIA RTX systems and around 30 milliseconds on NVIDIA L40 GPUs.

The target is news teams. They can use the score to prioritize review, flag or quarantine suspicious footage, and pass it on for deeper analysis. Nvidia was careful to say this doesn't replace existing verification processes — it only provides “another signal.”
It runs on-premises, at the edge, in hybrid setups, and in approved air-gapped environments. It's also being integrated into partner software such as the Wowza Video Intelligence Framework.

blocks.cap: Motion Picture Association CEO Charles Rivkin (Photo: Jerod Harris/Getty Images for CinemaCon)

blocks.x: The agreement spans ByteDance's Seedance video model and several other products, including TikTok.

Six months after a fully AI-generated video pitting Tom Cruise against Brad Pitt swept the internet, the technology that made the fake has been fitted with safeguards for Hollywood's intellectual property and likenesses.

The Motion Picture Association said Monday it had signed a memorandum of understanding with Chinese tech company ByteDance, putting “robust guardrails” to protect Hollywood inside the company's technology and platforms.
That covers Seedance, the AI video model that produced the Cruise-versus-Pitt clip, as well as Seedream 5.0 Lite, TikTok, CapCut and Dreamina.

Seedance's launch and the agreement that followed mirror OpenAI's video model Sora. Sora, too, was flooded with unauthorized videos of famous characters and people right after its release last year, and interest cooled once OpenAI moved to curb those fakes. Sora shut down earlier this year.
ByteDance is different. It keeps investing in Seedance, and the model ranks among the most advanced video models alongside rivals including Google's.

MPA chairman and CEO Charles Rivkin said in a statement: “Today's agreement reflects our belief that copyright is the cornerstone of the film and television industry, and it reaffirms our commitment to protecting creative content. Over the past several months, we have engaged constructively with ByteDance to put meaningful guardrails into Seedance and Seedream, and this memorandum of understanding carries our resolve to strengthen those guardrails together.”

ByteDance's general counsel John Rogovin added: “ByteDance respects the intellectual property rights that underpin the creative industries worldwide, and we believe responsible innovation in AI goes hand in hand with meaningful protections for rights holders. We continue to engage productively with the MPA and its member companies, strengthening safeguards across our generative AI services. This memorandum of understanding is an important framework for continuing that cooperation across products and platforms as the technology evolves.”

blocks.cap: Robin Williams (Photo: Frederick M. Brown/Getty Images)

blocks.x: A little more than a month after the late Robin Williams's 75th birthday, his three children reopened his Instagram account, honoring his legacy and pushing back against “rampant AI abuse” of his likeness.

Zak, Zelda and Cody Williams posted a joint statement to the actor's Instagram on Monday. “We're grateful to see a new generation discover our dad's work, and longtime fans continue to celebrate the joy he brought. As the technology changes, we hope this space stays safe and trustworthy, so that the stories, photos, videos and memories shared here honor his legacy with authenticity, warmth and care. It's our way of sharing his singular talent and humor with the world, down to the moments that made us — and so many of you — laugh. He continues to inspire us and bring joy to people around the world.”

Zelda Williams, the Oscar-winning comedian's eldest daughter, elaborated on the reasoning in an Instagram Story on her own account, acknowledging that the account's return could be a “trigger” for some fans.

“I know it's weird, honestly,” she wrote. “Making this a place where people can find real clips and photos of him is one of the best ways we've found right now to counter the rampant AI abuse of his voice and likeness happening here.”

With unauthorized AI deepfakes flooding the internet for living and deceased celebrities alike, people and their families have had to figure out how to put verified images front and center. Williams's Instagram account had sat dormant since his death in 2014.

This isn't the first time Zelda Williams has spoken out against unauthorized use of her father's likeness. Last October, she asked people sending her AI videos of her father to “stop doing this to him, to me, or just in general.”

“It's dumb, it's a waste of time and energy, and believe me, it's not honoring him,” she wrote in an Instagram Story at the time. “Watching the legacy of a real person be condensed into ‘well, it kind of looks and sounds like them, that's good enough,’ especially when it's just other people doing a puppeteering routine to make awful TikTok slop, is maddening.”
She made similar remarks during the 2023 SAG-AFTRA strike, calling AI videos using her father's voice “personally disturbing.”

“These recreations are at best, a poor facsimile of better people's talents, and at worst, a Frankensteinian monster stitching together the worst pieces of this industry, not aiming for what it should be,” she wrote.

blocks.cap: A test of Descript's a/v translation and dubbing lip-sync (Image: ProVideo Coalition)

blocks.x: I'm fluent in both Castilian and English, but other languages are a different story. With Descript, I look and sound like I'm fluent in French, German, and Greek.

I've reviewed Descript's other features several times and still use them often, but this is the first time I've tried out its a/v translation and dubbing. Native-speaker editing is only available on the Business or Enterprise plans, and I'm on the Creator plan. Descript doesn't stop at translating and dubbing — it matches the speaker's mouth shape with surprising accuracy. My first guess was that it must be rotoscoping. Looking into it, I found that Descript says it's not rotoscoping — it generates the lip-sync with generative AI. Running translate-and-dub doesn't just produce a new voiceover; it redraws the lower part of the speaker's face to follow the sounds, the particular breathing, and the mouth movements of the new language.

It's not done by tracing frame by frame. First, the original video and reference frames of the speaker's face are compressed and encoded into a trained latent space. Then it takes the translated audio and regenerates the lower face, keeping the original lighting, teeth, and the speaker's identity intact while only letting the speech follow the new language. Finally, it blends the newly generated mouth movement seamlessly with the untouched areas, like the background or the upper part of the face.

The test ran US English and Castilian Spanish originals, each translated into Canadian French, European French, German, and Greek. The Castilian version was included to see whether changing the source language improved the result for a given target language. The original clips came from my earlier review of the OBSBOT Meet Flip 4K UHD/1080p/720p camera.

Call it rotoscoping or call it generative AI, the lip-sync results Descript's translate-and-dub produces are impressive. As a certified translator, though, I don't sign off on machine translation that hasn't been edited by a native speaker. It's honestly frustrating that the Creator plan gives no way to edit the automatic translation before it runs. I'm not asking for a professional translator to be assigned. I just want the option to bring in my own translator to polish it. I hope that option comes to the Creator plan soon. For now, upgrading to the Business plan is the only way. Congratulations are due for the lip-sync results, though.

ComfyUI has shipped an official MCP. Claude or Codex can now write, run, and fix ComfyUI workflows directly. The model handles the node wiring, and the person making things only has to hold onto the creative half.

The team behind the video rates their own skill, generously, as "Comfy caveman" level at best. Even so, they call ComfyUI the single most important tool in the generative image and video space. It can make almost anything, but it takes time to learn. Their observation is that people who handle it well think half like an artist and half like an engineer. Now you can hand off that engineer half.

What you need is minimal: Claude Desktop or a ChatGPT Desktop that can use Codex, plus the ComfyUI desktop app. In exchange, you have to accept an agent touching your computer. The machine can be almost any recent PC or Mac, but a PC with an Nvidia card somewhere between a 4090 and a 5090 causes less trouble. The demo in the video ran on a 5090. If you don't have the hardware, you can use Comfy Cloud or rent an H100 on RunPod for $3.29 an hour.

The install instructions are almost absurdly short. Tell Claude to install ComfyUI MCP — both the community version and the official version — in a single line, and that's it. The official MCP is still in beta, so the advice is to keep the long-running community version around and switch to it when you hit a wall.

Tokens need to be used carefully. He attaches cheap models as sub-agents and runs them like hands and feet, while reserving the expensive model for supervision. Things like tweaking a prompt or extending a video's length from 124 frames to 248 frames are better done by hand.

When he actually told Claude to build an entire image-to-video workflow from scratch, a graph came out. Generation took 204 seconds, a bit over three minutes, and since it all ran locally, it cost nothing at all. Using API nodes, you can also mix in closed models like Seedance 2.5 or Topaz within the same graph; that side isn't local and costs credits. When he found a LoRA that looked promising, just dropping in the address was enough for it to install itself.

His parting point is simple: open-source video models are quickly catching up to the latest commercial models, and the cost of closed platforms keeps rising. If something can be solved locally, it's better to do it locally. Of the two barriers to entry, this MCP has, for now, knocked down the learning curve.

Eddie AI published research showing that even a 9-billion-parameter model can compete with much larger frontier models at video editing. The student model Qwen3.5-9B, trained through knowledge distillation, beat Kimi K3 47% of the time in head-to-head short-form social video editing matchups. Kimi K3 has 2.8 trillion parameters.

blocks.cap: Eddie AI

blocks.x: Moonshot AI's Kimi K3 served as the teacher model. The untouched 9B model was initially picked only about 10% of the time in comparisons. After LoRA training, that rose to 32%, and after refining the trajectories, it reached 47%.

Instead of just piling on more training data, curating the trajectories was what worked. They extracted reasoning traces from the frontier model, filtered down to the better examples using best-of-N sampling, and repeatedly retrained on the student model's best outputs. In the process, reasoning length shortened by about 30%, which also cut inference costs.

blocks.cap: Eddie AI in action

blocks.x: The company is upfront about the limits, too. These are preliminary results confined to just over 100 real projects and one narrow task. The 47% figure comes from short-form social editing, not video editing as a whole. Only 10 pairs were evaluated by humans, and while that mostly matched the automated judging, it's a small validation sample.

The usefulness comes from the size. The quantized 9B model runs on a single workstation GPU. Running it on-premises means footage never has to leave the building. For broadcasters, sports rights holders, and production environments bound by NDAs or cloud restrictions, that condition is decisive.
CEO Shamir Allibhai put it this way: "Our customers aren't against AI training. They're against losing control over the knowledge they created."
Adobe has made changes to Firefly. It expanded the audio features, added more external AI models, and opened up the Firefly AI Assistant so it can be used for free as well.
Generate Music, Generate Speech, and Generate Sound Effects have all become official features. They were built with video and social content, ads, shorts, tutorials, and podcast clips in mind.

Generate Music creates a new track to match a video's length and mood. Generate Speech turns a script into a voiceover, letting you choose between Adobe's own voice model and ElevenLabs. Generate Sound Effects creates sound effects matched to the action and timing on screen.

blocks.cap: Adobe Generate Music

blocks.x: Adobe cited a recent survey it ran with Berklee College of Music. "79.3% of respondents said they post video content daily or several times a week, and 100% said they use music in their videos." As obstacles, they named "legal and copyright risk at 43.2%, and licensing costs at 38.9%."

The Firefly AI Assistant, which debuted in beta earlier this year, also got an easier entry point. It includes features like Create Storyboard and Create Brand Kit, and a free trial with a set daily generation limit is now open.

blocks.cap: Firefly AI Assistant

blocks.x: The lineup of models available inside Firefly has also grown. Models from Adobe, Google, Kling AI, Luma AI, OpenAI, Runway, and others are on the list. The newest addition, Gemini Omni Flash, accepts not just text but video, audio, and images as input too. Adobe explained that with this model, you can set a video concept inside Firefly and refine it gradually.

This follows the earlier addition of Runway Aleph 2.0 and Kling 3.0. Adobe's explanation is that gathering multiple AI models and creative tools in one place, Firefly, lets people pick a different model for each task without switching apps or subscriptions.

Director James Gray doesn't mince words when AI comes up. Calling the AI filmmaking the industry is now pushing “obscene,” he said in a recent IndieWire interview that he has become convinced this trend will ultimately fail.

blocks.cap: James Gray at the Cannes Film Festival press conference for “Paper Tiger.” Getty Images

blocks.x: On the upcoming Filmmaker Toolkit podcast, he said this: “I'm weirdly optimistic. If you don't already know it, you'll know it soon. AI cannot touch the infinite layers of the soul. It would be great if it sped up medical trials for the people who need that. But who we really are, our souls, are the only truly infinite thing. What movies reach for, and really what all creation reaches for, is an unending mystery, endlessly layered. So what does that mean? It means imperfection is part of the equation.”

The same theme ran through the entire conversation about his new crime drama “Paper Tiger.” He sees beauty and humanity in “flawed” images. “Once you get technically excellent, you lose the imperfection of the medium, the imperfection that creates a kind of magic. What people actually mean when they say ‘movie magic’ are things you would never do if you isolated them: an actor slightly out of focus, rough grain, a frame where you can't see the whole face, concealing some aspect of the body.”

He put going to a museum to see Van Gogh's brushstrokes on the same footing as watching an image shot on celluloid. “It's magic. That's what we're reaching for with film grain, reaching for our humanity.”

He also reversed something he told IndieWire in 2022. He now regrets shooting his last film, “Armageddon Time,” digitally. Because the film leaned on performances from young actors, he felt he needed the freedom to repeat long takes, and the choice was his to make. He's still proud of the film itself and of Darius Khondji's cinematography, but he felt something was missing throughout the shoot. “I fought and fought to get imperfection out of digital, to get the grain, the elusiveness and irreversibility of the image.”

He also points to how “disposable” digital images have become. “More photos are being taken than ever. But people aren't looking at them. Have you ever watched a teenager scroll through an Instagram feed?” Photographs carry a moment you can never get back, he says, and film turns that irreversibility into beauty. “If a movie looks like a football broadcast, it'll bother your eyes. It's too vivid. It has none of the beauty of the past.”

On “Paper Tiger,” Gray and cinematographer Joaquín Baca-Asay went back to celluloid, using vintage lenses and gear, tungsten lighting in particular. He doesn't see this sensibility as his alone. He compares it to the return of the 12-inch record in music. “My kids know it, and young people know it. That's why vinyl came back. In the ‘80s and early ‘90s everything went digital, and then one day people listened to records and said, ‘wait, this is better.’ Because the signal stays continuous. When the needle sits in the groove, the signal never breaks, but digital splits it into zeros and ones. That imperfection, that warmth, reminds us of who we are.”
“Paper Tiger” was chosen as this year's New York Film Festival opening film, and NEON will put it in theaters on November 13, 2026.

AI-based animation software company MetaBull has acquired the studio Inkrise. Alongside the acquisition, an in-house production division called MetaBull Labs has been formed, and Aaron Simpson continues on as head of production.

blocks.cap: (From left) Dr. Topher Taylor, Aaron Simpson, Lyle Holmes. Image courtesy of MetaBull

blocks.x: MetaBull's founding team includes CEO Lyle Holmes, who came through Amazon Prime Video and Disney streaming; Emmy-winning producer Dr. Topher Taylor, who worked at Nelvana and Cookie Jar Entertainment; and AI specialist Dr. Iyanu Odebode.

The lineup and partnerships Inkrise was running move over to MetaBull Labs. This organization handles partner services, co-productions, and development of its own IP, and carries projects all the way from script breakdown to 4K delivery.

Simpson previously served as VP of Disney TV Animation development and as a producer at Warner Bros. Animation. He developed 'Johnny Test' and received an Emmy nomination as producer of 'Coconut Fred's Fruit Salad Island.' He made a name for himself by creating the Flash animation news site 'Cold Hard Flash,' and served as executive producer on the Telly Gold Award–winning PBS Kids show 'Weather Hunters.'

The company highlights two tools. The Felix production pipeline is built around USD and handles scene assembly, layout, camera blocking, and previsualization inside standard DCC software. The AIR pipeline turns layout, storyboard, and animation data into finished footage. Because the rendering is deterministic, story continuity and characters don't drift.

Both systems exchange data with major studios following the OpenUSD framework and the 2026 VFX reference standard. MetaBull emphasizes that it built its platform on ethically sourced datasets and studio-owned libraries with intact copyright provenance.

blocks.cap: Verena Puhm — Courtesy photo

blocks.x: Filmmaker and former Luma AI executive Verena Puhm has opened production company Matriarch in Los Angeles.
Puhm most recently led Dream Lab LA at Luma AI. She now develops and produces AI-native and hybrid productions directly, while also taking on third-party and brand work.

Matriarch's development slate includes the hybrid drama series “Colors in the Dark,” the adult animated comedy series “All the Leading Men,” the horror feature “G-Pigs,” and the animated short-form series “Chomper Romp,” which is currently in financing discussions.

Creative collaborators include director and AI creator-musician TEDRA (TT The Artist), whose credits include work with Diplo and Alicia Keys as well as Netflix, HBO's “Insecure,” “P-Valley,” and Lena Waithe's “Twenties”; music producer Joachim M. Weber, formerly a composer and audio designer at ProSiebenSat.1; and David Sulpizio, a creative technologist as well as director, producer, and VFX artist.
Producer Morenike Dosu, who joins Puhm at the self-funded company, has worked at MPC, Framestore, and DreamWorks Animation. Consultants include James Stowe and Courtney Pimster.

“We're building a studio shaped around where entertainment is heading,” Puhm said. “The core business is storytelling. We develop our own IP and produce projects for partners. But we build technology alongside that work, not by setting up a traditional studio structure and bolting on technology later.”

At the center of the new technology work is what the company calls “Affective Content Intelligence,” Matriarch's proprietary approach to understanding how audiences respond to media. According to the company, it is developing a system that combines biometric signals, self-reported emotional intent, and information about content watched to map the relationship between entertainment and emotional or physiological response. Rather than relying solely on clicks, completion rates, and traditional audience research, it is exploring using audience response as another input into creative development, content discovery, and greenlight decisions.

“Most entertainment technology is built to predict what you'll watch next,” Puhm said. “We want to know what you want to feel, how a given work affects you, and what can be learned from that response. When that intelligence connects directly to a studio, it changes not just discovery but what gets made.”

Puhm was lead AI artist on the 2025 Sundance documentary “Free Leonard Peltier.” She worked as a writer at Leonine Studios' Wiedemann & Berg TV and Red Bull Media's Terra Mater Studios, and co-directed and co-produced the 2023 documentary “Disaster at Devil's Jaw.” She was also an early AI filmmaking instructor at Sundance Collab.

blocks.cap: Rick Baker with his Locarno 2026 award — Courtesy of Locarno Film Festival/Ti-Press

blocks.x: Rick Baker, a seven-time Academy Award winner for makeup, has now added the Golden Leopard to his collection. It's one more item to place beside a lifetime of bizarre creatures. On Wednesday evening at the 79th Locarno Film Festival, the Vision Award presented by Ticinomoda went to him.

“Rick Baker is a man who brought about a Copernican revolution in cinema. He opened a new path for an entire generation's imagination, and showed what it truly means to witness a physical transformation on the big screen.” Those were the words of Locarno artistic director Giona A. Nazzaro in announcing the award.

Asked how he views the rise of AI, Baker brought up the era when computers and CGI first emerged. “People told us we'd suddenly become dinosaurs. But what was made on computers back then was pretty bad. My work clearly looked better than '90s computer graphics, and it still holds up today.”

Still, he believed the old and the new could coexist. “It was just a new toy, and I hoped people would move past the excitement and the two techniques would find a good combination. CGI clearly does things people can't. That's what I was looking forward to.”

He added that he'd always tried to keep up with new technology. “One of my first idols, Jack Pierce, created Frankenstein, the Wolf Man, and the Mummy, and got fired from Universal in the '40s. He couldn't keep up with modern techniques. While other studios were using foam appliances, he was still building up shapes on actors' faces with spirit gum and cotton. I burned that into my head and said, ‘That's not going to happen to me.’”

On CGI itself, he said this. “The work being done with CGI these days is amazing. What I dislike is when CGI is used for something that could actually be done, and more cheaply, practically. When an actor looks in the mirror and the face looking back is no longer their own, that's where the real magic is.”

His experience working with Eddie Murphy on “Coming to America” backs that up. “We had to turn Murphy into Saul, an old white Jewish man. I always test makeup before shooting. There were about 14 pieces. What won Eddie over right away was that even though the cheek pieces painted in white skin tone looked really strange, he looked in the mirror and moved his face around, played with it. That told me he wasn't the kind of actor who'd say ‘I can't move’ once something was glued on.”

Murphy looked into the mirror and said, “Rick, this is so much better than I imagined. It really looks like the guy. The old Jewish character I do is a total stereotype.” Murphy wanted to try improvising scenes while still in the test makeup. “From then on, that became how we worked. Every time we did makeup, I'd sit him in the chair, he'd play around, I'd shoot, and he'd discover the character. It's really different from walking into a green screen room with dots on your face.”

Baker also said Hollywood's “below-the-line” work still doesn't get the respect it deserves. “A hobby turned into a career, and it let me make things I never could have made alone. I gripe about the film industry sometimes, but it's been good to me. Unfortunately, the people who do this work because they love the craft are exactly the ones called below-the-line. The above-the-line people only care about how much money they can make.”
Baker's closing words: “The people who really care are the below-the-line people, and they're the ones who actually make the movie.”

blocks.cap: Image credit: Strada

blocks.x: Strada 2.0 mounts a collaborator's storage as a virtual drive inside macOS Finder or Windows Explorer. The remote editor cuts using media that never leaves the ingest disk.

Strada is a company founded in 2023 by brothers Michael Cioni (formerly of Frame.io and Adobe) and Peter Cioni (formerly of Netflix). It started out as an AI media search tool, but customer feedback shifted the direction. The bottleneck wasn't searching footage — it was reaching all of it in the first place.

When a collaborator invites a folder or an entire drive, that folder appears in Finder like a local volume. You browse it, preview it, and drag it straight into Premiere Pro, DaVinci Resolve, Photoshop, or Pro Tools. There's no uploading, no downloading, and no third-party bucket sitting between the two machines.

Underneath it all is Strada Agents, the P2P layer unveiled at NAB 2025. The agent runs on the computer holding the media and exposes connected storage to approved users. It works with internal drives, DAS, RAID, and NAS, as well as camera cards, with no dedicated hardware required. Opening a clip transfers only the bytes needed for playback and scrubbing, and a cache builds up locally as the session continues.

An actual project is a better reference point than a booth demo. Ryan Connolly of Film Riot edited “Work in Progress,” a short made with Fujifilm, using Strada Connect. The source was roughly 7TB, and the team worked about 1,500 miles apart in Premiere Pro over home internet connections. Connolly says it played back like local footage and he couldn't tell the difference.

blocks.cap: Credit: Strada

blocks.x: 2.0 bundles the features into four. Connect handles the virtual drive and remote editing; Transfer handles direct machine-to-machine transfers, with bandwidth limits and checksum reports attached. Upload Links closes the loop the other way: you create a folder link and send it, and the recipient uploads directly with no account needed. Permissions come in five roles at the folder level.

The core claim in the security documentation is that media is never stored or cached on Strada's cloud at any point. The servers only handle authentication and connection brokering, and files stay on the customer's hardware. Peer connections authenticate with Ed25519 keys generated locally on the device. If an agent is offline, a remote session can't be established, and pulling the drive air-gaps the media on the spot. SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001 are still in progress.

Strada's position is that it sells a protocol, not storage, and pricing is per seat. The company's comparison table assumes 5 users and 20TB, putting itself at $150 a month or $1,800 a year, against cloud alternatives that meter storage at $595 to $1,500 a month. Since the company picked the scenario, it's better read as a directional comparison.

There are two constraints. One is bandwidth: because it's P2P, the host machine's upload speed becomes the ceiling for everyone pulling that media. Feeding three editors over a single asymmetric home connection is a different matter from serving one proxy. The other is uptime: the source computer has to stay awake and logged in, so an editor's workstation quietly becomes infrastructure. Linux support exists only on the roadmap.
The free tier covers unlimited device and storage connections plus asset browsing. Basic adds remote editing and unlimited transfers for $8 a month, and Pro is $24 a month.

blocks.cap: ‘As Deep as the Grave’ — FirstLine Films

blocks.x: The period drama “As Deep as the Grave,” which drew attention for casting an AI version of the late Val Kilmer, has released nearly seven minutes of footage showing what that technology produces.

In the IndieWire-exclusive clip, Kilmer's AI-made character, Father Fintan, travels across a Navajo reservation searching for the source of an evil spirit sickening the land. His guide is Jonathan Nez, a former president of the Navajo Nation. Set in the early 20th century, Father Fintan is trying to raise money to build a new church by collecting relics.

Kilmer, who died in 2025 from throat cancer, was originally cast in the film. He was reportedly drawn strongly to the fact that it's set in New Mexico and the American Southwest, where he made his home. Delays from Covid and then his declining health meant he never made it to set. Instead, his family, including his children Mercedes and Jack, agreed to let AI create a digital version of their father, and the production paid his estate under SAG guidelines.
“I hope this helps lay the groundwork for how to do this properly,” said Coert Voorhees, who wrote and directed the film. “This work is about consent, collaboration, and compensation.”

On screen, Kilmer looks close to his prime in the 1990s. Voorhees said he shaped the performance by poring over “Heat,” “Batman Forever,” and “Tombstone.” “I tried to become the best student of Val there is. I watched ‘Heat’ literally ten times. Scrolling through footage, I saw a moment of him walking, and it was unmistakably Doc Holliday.”

blocks.cap: ‘As Deep as the Grave’ — FirstLine Films

blocks.x: Producer and brother John Voorhees said the AI work results in “a performance as close as possible to what Val would have wanted for this character.” “My brother spends an enormous amount of time matching even a single mole on the left side of the jaw.”

These scenes were chosen because they reveal the young Father Fintan and because the dramatic arc is alive in them. “Once you get through the seven minutes, you can see him wrestling between two identities. He's a Catholic priest and he's of Cherokee descent.”

The AI-made Kilmer currently appears for “roughly” one hour and 17 minutes out of a runtime that now exceeds three hours. The production combines younger images the family provided from their personal archive with footage from his later years to depict the character across decades. The voice draws on late-life recordings that had been affected by a tracheostomy. Live-action footage of Abigail Lawrie, Tom Felton, Wes Studi, and Abigail Breslin is mixed with the AI elements.

Since showing a trailer at CinemaCon last spring, the team has spent the whole summer working on Kilmer's scenes. “It's labor-intensive. Right up until a clip goes out, some shots made Val look a bit older and some made him look younger. You have to go through all of it and make it consistent. Every single beat matters.”

Given how central AI is, the budget is small. The technology cost, by John Voorhees' account, is “a few thousand dollars.” “It's shockingly cheap, and it helps us as people making an independent film.”

The brothers say buyer interest has been strong. “We've had meetings with streamers, and honestly they're the ones learning from us, since we're still the only film with an A-list star appearing as an AI character with their own consent.” They hope streamers eyeing the film as an example of combining well-made generative AI performance with in-camera footage is where this ends up.

The brothers believe this kind of production could also help other celebrities' estates. “We love people from the past and want to stay connected to them. But there has to be consent and compensation.”

blocks.cap: AccuFACE 2

blocks.x: Reallusion has released AccuFACE 2, a markerless facial motion capture system. It's a production-grade tool that transfers facial performance shot with an ordinary webcam or iPhone camera directly onto CC5 HD characters, with no separate mocap studio required.
Since it extracts character expressions from footage alone, with no markers or helmet rigs, it's aimed squarely at small animation teams that don't have a mocap stage.
The core of the tool is that, instead of expensive equipment, a webcam or smartphone already sitting on the desk is enough to capture facial performance the very next day.

LTX has released LTX-2.5, an open-weight video world model. Just as a large language model predicts the next word, a world model predicts the next moment in a video. Studios can run this model on their own servers, keeping footage and IP in-house, and even fine-tune it further on their own material.

blocks.cap: LTX-2.5

blocks.x: There are three key points. It renders multi-shot sequences at once while keeping characters, backgrounds and voices consistent across cuts. It fully supports reading and writing ACES HDR, preserving tonal range through the entire production pipeline. And it carries its own Gemma 4 language backbone plus a dedicated prompt enhancer, letting it handle complex prompts with multiple subjects tangled together.

Technically, it uses a method called Diffusion Fidelity Rendering. It builds motion and structure in a latent space compressed 8x, and sets up high-quality keyframes by adjusting the number of key frames to match scene complexity and available compute. A new decoder keeps the same compression efficiency while reducing artifacts in high-motion scenes.

It's available immediately through Hugging Face, the LTX API and ComfyUI. LTX co-founder and CEO Zeev Farbman said, "A world model grapples with a problem large language models have never faced: keeping motion, space and sound consistent over time." Cumulative downloads have passed 33 million, and it's already being used in film production, robotics and real-time rendering, with partners including Asteria, ComfyUI, Markov Robotics and Reactor.
Runway Ruby is a new model that creates 16-bit HDR ProRes and EXR sequences. It can also convert clips you've already shot, or earlier generated output, into that format.
It works alongside other video models, including Gen-4.5, Seedance 2.5, and MiniMax H3.
You can try Runway Ruby today at app.runwayml.com.

ProFuzz Digital has expanded the speech-to-text features in SubtitleNext, its subtitle and audio-description management platform. It now connects four AI transcription engines — AssemblyAI, Deepgram, ElevenLabs, and Whisper — so users can choose based on language coverage, accuracy, processing speed, and deployment method.

blocks.cap: SubtitleNext

blocks.x: On the localization side, it added import and export support for the IMSCR script format, along with more integrations tied to production and localization pipelines. The display now supports HiDPI for high-resolution screens, and users can customize workspace columns per project.

Batch processing also expanded. Burn-in jobs, duplicate/delete functions, and timecode conversion with offset adjustment can all run together, and a new Movie File Burn Expert plugin converts video across multiple formats and resolutions. On the broadcast side, Teletext validation coverage was expanded, and a speaker-role assignment feature for accessibility work was added.

ProFuzz Digital CEO Ivanka Vasileva said, “We understand how important the role of subtitle creators is across sports content, film, and TV programming.” The update is set to be demonstrated at IBC 2026.

Curious Refuge's weekly AI movie news show, 'Apple Can Now Clone You and it's CRAZY Realistic.' Released August 21, 2026, running about 33 minutes. It opens with Seedance 2.5's 1080p update alongside Runway, Artlist and Dreamina, then covers a memorandum of understanding between the Motion Picture Association (MPA) and ByteDance on IP protection, Apple's face and emotion cloning research 'Heads Up', the open-source voice cloning tool Index TTS 2.5, Move AI's motion capture system 'M3', Lottielab, CADxstudio, and this week's AI short film.

The video centers on a new white paper from Apple's research team. The tool, called Heads Up, is still internal to Apple and not a publicly released product. The team gathered 10,000 subjects and photographed their faces in high resolution. From those photos they built 3D Gaussian splats, essentially high-resolution 3D scans that let you rotate the camera freely around them. That's where it starts.

The real part comes next. By blending the images of the 10,000 subjects, the system synthesizes new faces from a simple prompt. It then projects emotion onto that 3D face, whether the face is real or synthesized. In the video, a man's exaggerated expression is lifted and placed onto a neutral scan of a woman below. It also works the other way: a single neutral scan takes on an entirely different person's expression. When a real actor performs on the left side of the screen, five people on the right mirror that same performance.

It doesn't stop there. Apple also built a UI that lets users fine-tune a character's expression. A person grabs sliders directly and pushes and pulls emotions. Tools like this have existed before, but Curious Refuge judges this level of detail and control to be the best available right now.

In day-to-day work, there isn't much need to fiddle with sliders to this degree. But inside Photoshop, it's a different story. When an ad shot with a model needs just a tiny tweak to its expression, or when a movie poster needs an emotion that wasn't captured on set, it's easy to picture this kind of technology settling into professional tools. This round of subjects was called into Apple's headquarters for scanning, but given the sensors already built into the iPhone, it looks like this could reach everyday users before long.

Brandon Tonner-Connolly, production designer on 'Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma,' broke down a glass matte painting shot in an entertaining Instagram post. Article by Ian Failes, August 24, 2026.

blocks.cap: A glass matte painting shot from 'Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma.' Image source: befores & afters

blocks.x: Tonner-Connolly's post begins with the idea that, since Camp Miasma is officially opening today, he wanted to take a closer look at that glass matte shot. It started as an idea to build a portal for Chris to walk into, and it turned into a project where a group of talented people made something no one had done before.

EditShare, a collaborative media storage and workflow vendor, is showing off new features spanning EFS, Flow AI, MediaSilo, and EditShare One at IBC 2026.

At the center is an all-in-one Ultimate configuration for the EFS 310 and EFS 410, which puts Flow media management and GPU-based Flow AI processing inside the node itself. That comes alongside expanded multilingual transcription, improvements to Flow AI and EditShare One, and a preview of what's next for MediaSilo.

blocks.cap: A diagram of the EditShare product lineup unveiled at IBC 2026.

blocks.x: “Production teams now have more storage platforms, locations, and collaboration tools to deal with than ever before,” said EditShare CEO Brad Turner. “We're focused on bringing those workflows closer together without locking customers into a closed ecosystem. What we're introducing at IBC connects high-performance storage, smart media discovery, and secure collaboration. It helps teams find content faster and push projects forward with less manual effort.”
Packing shared storage, media management, and AI processing into one box means even teams that don't need a dedicated GPU system can easily get access to AI media discovery.
Flow AI analyzes audio and video to generate searchable, structured metadata. It searches dialogue and transcripts, identifies scenes and faces, detects logos, and reads on-screen text.

Processing finishes entirely on-premises. Since content never has to go to an outside AI service, the company keeps control of security, privacy, and data governance. Pricing is also an unlimited flat rate with no per-minute or usage-based charges, so teams can analyze as much as the system can handle.

Supported transcription languages grow to 13: English, Catalan, Croatian, Czech, Danish, Dutch, French, German, Greek, Italian, Portuguese, Spanish, and Turkish, with Hebrew and Arabic coming soon. Broadcasters, production companies, and post teams can now sweep even international content with AI search. Tagged people and logos also show up more clearly on the media player timeline.

MediaSilo is expanding beyond a review-and-approval tool into a production media hub. With the new connected-storage feature, Media Drives, authorized users can reach approved S3-compatible storage directly from MediaSilo. That includes on-premises EFS exposed via S3 and supported third-party platforms.

blocks.cap: A screen from Media Drives, MediaSilo's new connected-storage feature.

blocks.x: Users can browse folders, find mounted media by filename, and preview it right where it's stored. Since only the files you need get copied, there's no need to move everything before you even know what you need. After moving files, MediaSilo AI lets you search transcripts, on-screen text, people, logos, and scenes, while the same workspace handles timecode feedback, version control, dailies, and approval tracking.

External collaborators can view content in a browser without joining the production network or using a VPN. Forensic and visual watermarking, DRM, expiration settings, permissions, download restrictions, and multi-factor authentication protect unfinished cuts and unreleased material.

EditShare One speeds up content access and management across EFS and Flow. Entire media spaces or folders can be archived and restored directly from here. Archive workflows now also support Telestream Diva Archive and Spectra Logic Rio MediaEngine integration, in addition to the third-party storage Flow already supports.
Apple introduced a new Mac Studio with the M5 Max and M5 Ultra on board. The company calls it “a monumental step forward for AI.” Given how Apple's recent announcements have gone, that's nothing new.

blocks.cap: The new Mac Studio models. Image courtesy of Apple.

blocks.x: Putting on-device AI front and center is also expected. But amid all the AI language, it's worth digging out what this Mac Studio actually does for ordinary video editing.

The headline numbers are still on the AI side. Apple says AI performance is 4.3 times faster. Alongside that are figures of up to 2 times for storage, 1.8 times for graphics, 1.3 times for CPU, and increased memory bandwidth. For editors, these are the more welcome numbers.

The M5 Max model has an 18-core CPU, a GPU with up to 40 cores and a neural accelerator in every core, and up to 128GB of unified memory. The M5 Ultra goes further, with up to a 36-core CPU, up to an 80-core GPU, and 512GB of unified memory.

“Mac Studio is the ultimate desktop for on-device AI and the world's most demanding pro workflows. It's been loved for sitting quietly on a desk in a small body while delivering tremendous performance and extensive pro connectivity. Today we've pushed those limits further.” That's from Apple's hardware engineering lead, Johny Srouji.
What stands out for film and editing is Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6, both making their first appearance in a Mac Studio. Thunderbolt 5 comes along with them.

The M5 Max is up to 10.7 times faster than the M1 Max, and 3.9 times faster than the M4 Max, on LLM prompt processing in LM Studio. For text-to-image, it's 7.4 times faster than the M1 Max and 3.5 times faster than the M4 Max. Magic Mask in Blackmagic Design DaVinci Resolve Studio is 5.3 times faster than the M1 Max and 3 times faster than the M4 Max. Pricing starts at $2,499.

The M5 Ultra is up to 15.4 times faster than the M1 Ultra, and 3.3 times faster than the M3 Ultra, on CopyCat ML training in Foundry Nuke. LM Studio prompt processing is 9.8 times faster than the M1 Ultra, text-to-image is 8.2 times faster, and Maxon Redshift scene rendering is 4.7 times faster. Pricing starts at $5,499.

Joseph Bell has released the third annual edition of the Visual Effects & Animation World Atlas, available free at vfxatlas.com. The 2026 edition covers more than 140,000 VFX and animation workers at 2,900 companies, and puts net employment growth at 2.7% over the past 12 months, up from 1% the year before.

blocks.cap: Cover of the Visual Effects & Animation World Atlas. Image courtesy of Joseph Bell.

blocks.x: Bell spent 20 years as a VFX producer and company executive at Industrial Light & Magic, The Mill, and FuseFX before releasing the first Atlas in 2024. The data gathered so far totals 1.1 million records, with more than 10,000 readers across 100 countries.

“Visual effects grew from a handful of companies into a multi-billion-dollar global industry in just two decades,” Bell said. “And yet it's still a poorly understood business. Market research reports costing thousands of dollars put the global workforce at a million people, and expert studies inflate the major-market workforce by 250%. These bad numbers travel straight into reputable media and industry decision-makers. The Atlas was built to correct that with data filtered through real-world experience.”

Los Angeles shrank 1.5% over 12 months, a smaller drop than the 1.8% the year before, and remains the largest hub when VFX and animation are combined. Vancouver rebounded 11.3%, Montreal held steady after losing more than half its workforce between 2022 and 2025, and Toronto slipped 3.3%. The title of world's largest VFX hub went to Mumbai, which grew 4%, while Chennai and Hyderabad are growing fastest at 10.8% and 7.8% respectively. Ireland grew 13.8%.

Major studios also came under scrutiny. “After Technicolor and MPC collapsed in February 2025, there was talk that one more global-scale VFX studio would fall before the industry stabilized,” Bell said. “The three biggest now are DNEG, Industrial Light & Magic, and Framestore, and together they employ 12.3% of the global workforce, up from 11% in 2025. The real threat isn't a shortage of work but the business environment, which is always tight. What brought down Technicolor wasn't a lack of demand but debt it couldn't handle.”

In 2023, DreamWorks Animation co-founder Jeffrey Katzenberg said the number of artists needed for a world-class animated film would drop from 500 to under 50 by 2026. “Comments like that spread the perception that VFX and animation industry employment has already been cut by AI,” Bell said. “The data shows no trace of that. AI-dedicated roles are the smallest slice in our dataset: 0.1% of traditional VFX and animation studio jobs in 2026. They are growing, though — up 68% over the past 12 months.”

“AI hasn't meaningfully replaced jobs at traditional VFX and animation studios, nor has it created them at any real scale. The effect is subtler: artists are adopting AI tools within the roles they already hold,” he added.

Roto and paint roles grew 8.7% over 12 months. The report reads this as a sign that AI hasn't taken over that work yet. Environment and DMP grew 9.3%, FX and simulation 6.1%, creature TD and CFX 5.2%, and business development 12%, while match move and tracking fell 1.3%. Remote work rose from 8.7% to 10%.
Bell now analyzes industry data through his own company, HDRI Intelligence.

WildBrain has completed its acquisition of Personality AI, a generative AI company that builds interactive character experiences for children. It paid about $11 million in cash plus 1 million shares of WildBrain stock, with another $2 million due a year later. Up to an additional $56 million could follow if revenue targets between 2027 and 2029 are met.

Founded in 2025, Personality AI builds conversational AI models for entertainment IP. Its flagship work is Hey Peppa Pig, an Amazon Kids+ app made with Hasbro, in which kids talk back and forth with Peppa while playing games and activities.

blocks.cap: Hey Peppa Pig promotional image.

blocks.x: WildBrain plans to apply this technology to its existing production, franchise management, and licensing business, building interactive experiences centered on its own IP and licensed brands.

In its announcement, the company emphasized child safety. The product maintains certification under the FTC-approved PRIVO COPPA Safe Harbor Program, with monitored conversations, usage limits, and age-appropriate content filters. WildBrain said it retains no children's voice data or personally identifiable information.

WildBrain President and CEO Josh Scherba said, “Personality AI lets fans connect with brands in a much more continuous way, and it strengthens our ability to offer partners end-to-end franchise solutions.”

Personality AI founder Jon Gosier will serve as Senior Vice President of the Personality AI division at WildBrain. He said, “We'll bring our capabilities to more brands, platforms, and audiences around the world while holding to a high standard of safety, trust, and innovation.”
This acquisition follows a less successful AI attempt. Restored episodes of The Super Mario Bros. Super Show! that aired on MeTV Toons showed noticeably blurred, uneven footage.
The investment comes about 11 months after WildBrain sold its remaining stake in Peanuts to Sony. That sale erased the company's debt and freed up $50 million to $100 million for growth investment.
Matt Wolfe called out Tencent's WorldClaw, saying it's among the most impressive AI models he's seen this year.
WorldClaw builds an entire 3D world from a single prompt. It doesn't just produce a backdrop — every object placed within it comes out separately.
Trees, buildings, carts, streetlights, even terrain are all generated as individual 3D assets. That means you can take them straight into your work and manipulate them.
Under the hood, image generation, segmentation, and Tencent's Hunyuan 2D-to-3D technology work together. The structure turns a single generated scene into a bundle of 3D objects.

The use cases are interesting too: pulling together a game environment in minutes, building a virtual world for simulation, or creating a space for a robot to train in before it heads into the real world.
It's not hands-on yet, though. Since it hasn't been released, Wolfe said he's watching and waiting too.

Autodesk's Flow Studio has moved beyond simply generating video from prompts. The new workflow targets something generative AI has rarely offered: control a director can actually touch.

blocks.cap: Autodesk Flow Studio's new 3D Editor and Canvas.

blocks.x: This episode of fxpodcast featured Nikola Todorovic, Wonder Dynamics co-founder now at Autodesk. The topic was Flow Studio's new 3D Editor and Canvas, which bundle together hands-on 3D scene building and the output of generative 2D video models.

The design intent isn't making a film from a single prompt. It's inserting AI into the production pipeline. It targets both individual filmmakers working in crews of three to five and much larger studios.

The premise is simple. Filmmakers direct in three dimensions: they place the camera, block actors, refine performances, and decide where a shot lands. Trying to convey all of that through text prompts or marks on a flat 2D image was always going to run into obvious limits.

In the 3D Editor, a shot is assembled from characters, animation, motion capture data, camera tracks, and generated environments. A performance can come from one reference clip, camera movement from another, or the camera can be keyframed directly. Spatially consistent environments, such as Gaussian splat worlds made with World Labs' Marble, are used for blocking, layout, and camera design.

Next comes Canvas, a node-based 2D environment where the final image is generated and refined. This is where today's AI video models already do well: integrating lighting, atmosphere, simulation effects, and a cinematic finish.

The 3D scene itself doesn't produce the final pixels. It sets the performance, staging, composition, and camera movement that guide the generated result. If speed matters, you can stay inside Canvas alone, and move into 3D only when a shot needs precise direction.

Todorovic talks about generative AI's 80/20 rule. A prompt and an AI model get the first 80 percent of an image done astonishingly fast. The problem comes when a director asks for a precise fix: move this object, change that performance, adjust the camera path, but don't touch what already looks good.

That last 20 percent is where prompt-only work becomes unpredictable. It's also where the “AI slop” criticism comes from. Without a way to reach directly into the shot, what artists get back is whatever interpretation the model judged statistically safest.

Hollywood filmmakers, executives, and actors have been meeting privately with Silicon Valley executives for the past three years, trying to settle a question the industry has carried for a long time: where does AI become useful within a creative process that people control?

blocks.cap: Photo: Getty Images for Disney.

blocks.x: The meetings were first convened by Lucasfilm's Kathleen Kennedy and American Film Institute dean Susan Ruskin, in November 2023. At a gathering of around 120 people last weekend, the coalition arrived at a single framework. It maps out where AI has already entered the film industry, sets out how people can retain control in the remaining use cases, and addresses the scope for AI to produce copyrightable work.

The framework was first reported by The Ankler. According to Page Six Hollywood, attendees included actor and InterPositive co-founder Ben Affleck, A24 partner Scott Belsky, CAA agent Greg Siegel, Paramount+ originals executive Chris Parnell, “Stutz” producer Diane Becker, 30 Ninjas CEO Zade Weintraub, and director John Avnet.

The document is called Human Generative Workflows. In its first public statement, the coalition said it was meant to “spark industry discussion and provide a shared vocabulary for thinking about authorship in the generative AI era.” It drew a line against tackling more urgent issues like how models are trained or how jobs will be affected.

“This conversation is bigger than AI,” the coalition said of the framework. “The future of entertainment won't be built by AI alone. It will be built by the choices we make about how to integrate AI into the creative process.”

The document first takes issue with how the industry talks about AI today, pointing out that the abbreviation “AI” covers everything from DaVinci Resolve's color grading assist to prompt-based synthetic performances that replace actors, in a single breath. So it proposes a classification system that sorts the AI already on set into categories, one that could eventually be used with audiences as well.
It also lists machine-learning-based tools that already produce copyrightable work. Items on the list of AI-assisted tasks include “upscaling and sharpening” and “markerless motion capture.”

The dividing line is AI-generated assets like voices and likenesses. The document defines these as tools that “replace human creative work,” distinguishing between “a set of tools and processes that serve a human's creative vision, versus prompt-based generative tools that replace it.” In the coalition's judgment, this latter category does not carry copyright.

Lineo, aimed at commercial production, has released a production management platform that runs a job from first bid to final wrap in one place. It covers budgets, calendars, bid letters, bid packages, purchase orders, payroll, and petty cash ledgers, with actual spend visible to the whole team in real time. It was built by working producers Corwin Carroll, Erik McCaslin, and Austin Beckford.

blocks.cap: Lineo's production calendar screen.

blocks.x: “Commercial production has never been squeezed harder than it is now. Deliverables keep growing, budgets keep shrinking,” says co-founder Carroll. “The only way out is working smarter. After more than a year of use by executive producers, line producers, and coordinators, Lineo has cut bidding time, which lets us work three times faster. We put that saved time back into the work itself.”

Production teams usually run on a dozen or so tools that don't talk to each other. Lineo says it has folded all of that into a single operating screen. At the bidding stage, producers build real-time, collaboratively edited budgets using the AICP/APA formats they already use, with support for the world's top 20 currencies. The planning stage brings calendars and resources onto one screen so the whole team sees the same picture.

At the package stage, you pull in a past budget, polish the bid letter with AI, brand the calendar, and export a single PDF bid package without ever leaving the app. At the settlement stage, AI scans and parses purchase orders, payroll, and petty cash to log them, and the result flows into actual spend figures that accounting software can read.

Production Assistant is an AI that pulls this job's data on the spot. “List unpaid purchase orders over $5,000.” “What's the deadline for the Taft-Hartley filing?” You can upload bid specs, scripts, and treatments and ask directly. Outside the assistant too, AI reads invoices, payroll documents, and receipts to fill in purchase order, payroll, and petty cash ledgers on its own, removing the window that used to produce the most mistakes at wrap.

The macOS desktop app runs fully offline. You can use it on a plane or on location and it syncs the moment you're back online. Security includes end-to-end encryption, tenant isolation with row-level permissions, payments handled only through Stripe, AI document processing that retains no data, and personal information that's automatically erased.

Pricing is split between an individual-producer plan and a production-team plan. Coming add-ons include ReelFlow, for sharing reels and libraries with collaborators, and Accounting Sync, for exporting directly to Xero and QuickBooks.

“After running a production company for a long time, what I needed most was for owners, executives, and accounting to see the situation in real time,” explains co-founder Beckford. “Because finding out a month later, there's nothing left you can do about it.”

Moonbug Entertainment, the children's content studio behind Cocomelon, Little Baby Bum, Blippi and Mia's Magic Playground, has asked its in-house animators to try using AI when making its shows, according to 404 Media.

blocks.cap: Moonbug Entertainment

blocks.x: A generative AI policy and a 'Studio AI Bible' obtained by 404 Media show the company is still in the early stages of experimentation, with multiple layers of guardrails set up because of the legal and copyright issues that come with deeper AI use.

“Keep a human in the loop when using AI. AI is a tool to assist the artist, not the artist,” one part of the guidelines reads. “Copyright only applies to human-made work. So the final output must contain substantial human creativity. Core IP — meaning primary characters, signature worlds, and important backgrounds — must reflect human creative intent.”

Moonbug's shows have hundreds of millions of subscribers on YouTube. A Cocomelon spinoff airs on Netflix, a Cocomelon movie with Universal is in the works, and the series is moving to Disney+ next year.

A spokesperson told 404 Media that “generative AI is not currently used in our content episodes.” The guidelines ban AI from generating major creative elements from scratch, such as new characters, core storylines, or song lyrics. All output goes through human-led quality control, including frame-by-frame visual review, the spokesperson said.

The guidelines allow AI in brainstorming, scriptwriting, storyboarding, design and animation, but attach conditions at every stage. Altering a voice actor's or performer's delivery without legal sign-off is not allowed. AI can polish a human-written draft but cannot ghostwrite one. Parts considered the 'soul' of the story — character arcs, key twists, and song lyrics — are left to humans. Feeding a 100% AI-made design straight into the production pipeline is also blocked.

The details are quite strict. AI can be used for 'generic' background designs and textures — like trees or furniture — swapping character outfits, and turning a human-drawn 2D character into a 3D turnaround. New characters are, in principle, made by humans. The same goes for unique props that get major attention in a series, like a clubhouse.

Each tool must receive individual legal approval. Employees first test tools on non-Moonbug-IP test assets. All AI use, including prompts, is logged and kept, and AI-made assets are stored in separate folders from human-made ones. The company calls this approach 'provenance and isolation.'

The prompt guide says to upload a human-drawn sketch or Moonbug-owned IP as a structural reference, then use AI to add texture and lighting. Text-to-image prompts are banned outside brainstorming and research. Style mimicry, such as “in the style of Pixar” or “in the style of Ghibli,” is also blocked. Instead, the guidance calls for descriptive language, like “hand-painted watercolor feel.”
Last May, IATSE workers on the live-action Cocomelon spinoff went on strike over wages and benefits.
“We see AI as a tool that expands what talented creators can do, not something that replaces the people who make the stories,” the spokesperson said.

blocks.cap: Avid Ready to Edit
